newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S ANC, IFP START CONSTITUTION TALKS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S ANC, IFP START CONSTITUTION TALKS.

text.p: South Africa's ruling ANC met leaders of Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's rival Inkatha party on Wednesday for talks on amending disputed portions of the new constitution.

The talks began at the parliament office of African National Congress chief negotiator and Secretary-General, Cyril Ramaphosa. ANC Constitutional Development Minister Mohammed Valli Moosa was also present.
The Inkatha Freedom Party, whose delegation was led by senior negotiator Ben Ngubane and hardline adviser, Walter Felgate, requested the meeting at the weekend.
Inkatha walked out of the constitution-making process 18 months ago in protest at the ANC's refusal to allow international mediation on their differences.
Inkatha demands strong autonomy for provincial governments but the ANC wants most power to be wielded by the central government.

The Constitutional Court this month rejected parts of the new constitution approved by parliament in May and sent them back for redrafting by the Constitutional Assembly, including those dealing with the powers of provinces.
This is the main point of contention.
Sub-committees of the Constitutional Assembly, made up of both houses of parliament and which wrote the draft law, are to meet at parliament from 10 a.m. (0800 gmt).

Buthelezi said on Sunday that in light of the court's decision Inkatha would meet the ANC to discuss the necessary amendments. But he stopped short of saying his party would participate in redrafting the constitution.
The Zulu-based Inkatha has majority support in KwaZulu-Natal province. An estimated 15,000 people have been killed there in a decade of feuding between Inkatha and the ANC.

A new version of the constitution must be submitted to the Constitutional Court by October 11 if it is to come into force in January, replacing an interim constitution adopted in the last days of the old apartheid government.
ANC leaders have said they are unwilling to let the IFP reopen negotiations over all aspects of the document. The Court said it expected only minor adjustments.
